notes.meaning: A worshiper could bring a grain offering to the Lord made of fine wheat flour, mixed with olive oil and topped with sweet frankincense. Unlike animal sacrifices, this gift involved no shedding of blood. It was a voluntary present to God, expressing gratitude for daily food and honoring Him as provider.

The worshiper brought the mixture to the priests, and a priest scooped up a handful of the flour and oil along with all the frankincense. This handful was burned on the altar as a memorial portion, sending up a pleasing aroma to the Lord. The burning portion served as a reminder that the whole gift, and indeed the worshiper's entire life, belonged to God.

The rest of the grain offering belonged to Aaron and the priests for their daily food. Because priests had no farmland of their own, God provided for them through the altar gifts. This food was called most holy, meaning only the priests could eat it, and only in the sacred courtyard.

If the grain offering was baked in an oven, it had to be made without yeast. The worshiper could bring thick loaves kneaded with olive oil, or thin wafers brushed with oil. God welcomed cooked food prepared with care in the home just as readily as raw flour.

A person could also bring bread cooked on a flat griddle over a fire, made of fine flour mixed with oil and without yeast. After baking, the worshiper broke the flatbread into pieces and poured more olive oil over it. This broken bread was then handed to the priest as a true grain offering to God.

The grain offering could also be cooked in a deeper pan, fried in oil until crisp. This gave people with different cooking tools the freedom to bring what they could prepare. God cared about a willing heart rather than the specific pan used.

Whichever way the bread was prepared, the worshiper brought it to the Tabernacle and handed it to the priest. The priest then carried it forward to the altar of burnt offering. God's house welcomed the fruits of everyday work brought in faith.

The priest broke off a memorial token from the cooked bread and burned it on the altar as a sweet aroma to the Lord. The entire remainder was set aside for Aaron and his sons as their holy portion. In this way, giving to God also supported those who served His people full-time.

No grain offering burned on the altar could contain yeast or honey. In the ancient world, yeast caused dough to sour and ferment, which often stood for sin, decay, or pride. Honey was also kept off the altar fire, likely because it fermented easily and was common in pagan worship.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Leaving out leaven and honey taught believers to keep double-dealing and bodily pleasures out of true worship, choosing instead a life of purity and self-denial.

notes.meaning: Offerings made with yeast or honey could still be brought as firstfruit gifts from the yearly crop, but they could never be burned on the altar fire. Instead, these gifts went straight to the priests for food. God made a clear line between what was burned directly for Him and what supported His servants.

Every grain offering had to be seasoned with salt, called here the salt of God's covenant. Salt preserves food from spoiling, so it stood for an enduring, unbroken friendship and covenant between God and His people. It was so important that God commanded salt to be placed on all sacrifices offered on the altar.

A worshiper could also bring a grain offering from the very first ripening grain of the field. Fresh, green ears of grain were roasted over the fire to dry them out, and then crushed into coarse meal. This gift was an early act of thanksgiving, trusting God to provide the rest of the harvest.

The worshiper poured olive oil over the crushed roasted grain and added frankincense, making it a complete grain offering. The priest then took a memorial handful of the grain and oil, along with all the incense, and burned it on the altar for the Lord. Giving the very first and best of the harvest showed deep honor to God before enjoying the rest.
